newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Italy, Commission meet on Alitalia rescue plan.
newsitem.headline: Italy, Commission meet on Alitalia rescue plan.

text.p: Italy and the European Commission tried on Wednesday to iron out differences about a plan to rescue loss-making airline Alitalia, but a final decision was not expected before the end of June.
European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock said after meeting Italian Industry Minister Claudio Burlando that progress had been made, but both declined to elaborate on the talks.

"We're having further technical discussions and it would be foolish for me to comment at this stage," Kinnock told reporters, adding: "Progress has been made, but there is a need for further in-depth discussions".
Italy requested EU permission last year for a capital injection worth some 3.3 trillion lire ($1.9 billion) into state-controlled Alitalia to prepare it for privatisation.

Alitalia's managing director Domenico Cempella, who also attended Wednesday's meeting, said recently the Commission had requested a reduction to 2.8 trillion lire. But Burlando declined to comment on the final figure.
Burlando's comments suggested that the two sides were still holding their positions.
"In our opinion this must be seen as a market investment plan," Burlando said, adding that Kinnock thought instead that it amounted to state aid.

At issue is whether Alitalia's parent, state-controlled industrial holding IRI, which is to bear the plan's cost, is acting as a private investor or whether the capital injection is a disguised subsidy.
The difference in views is far from academic and could lead to tougher conditions if Kinnock sticks to his position.
Burlando said he would meet Kinnock again at the end of May and hoped for a final Commission ruling at the end of June.

Alitalia, which chalked up its ninth straight year of losses in 1996, agreed to a rescue package with unions last June after a long and bitter battle over plans to slash personnel costs and boost productivity.
Wednesday's meeting was prompted by Kinnock's recent demand that changes be made to the plan, prompting bitter remarks by Cempella in Italy that the Commission was "prejudiced" against Alitalia.

Cempella said at the time that Kinnock's services had already told the company to alter some of its proposals forcing the group to shed 14 aircraft in 1997 and reduce its overall fleet size to 158 by the year 2000 instead of a planned 172.
The Commission has come under fire for clearing rescue packages to state-controlled airlines, particularly Air France which has received 20 billion francs since 1994.
